h: Exercise 2. A first blockout of your own idea
x: // start here Start: the first step Everything you need to join the year: what the club is about, what to install, and your first exercise — no computer needed. # What this club is about This year we don’t learn one program. We learn to see simple shapes in any object , to break the complex into simple parts and to assemble our own models from them — characters, vehicles, weapons, buildings, game props. Once this skill is sharp, moving from one 3D editor to another is easy: the buttons change, the thinking doesn’t. Three rules hold the year together: The idea is yours. Everyone works on their own idea, not the same task for everybody. The difficulty adapts to your level; the topic doesn’t. Every block ends with an artifact. Not an exercise for its own sake, but a thing you can show: from your first colored object to a model in augmented reality on your phone. No experience needed. If you have already tried modeling, every block has a “challenge” for you. The ceiling is open, the entry barrier is low. # What to install Blender — free 3D software that runs on an ordinary computer. We use Blender 5.2 LTS: download it from blender.org . A phone (iOS or Android) is only needed in block 8 , when your own model appears “on the table” in AR. Tip Follow the club’s announcements: the schedule, changes and materials are posted in the club’s Telegram group — the club leader provides the invitation. This site is the permanent place where all materials and exercises live. # Exercise 1. See the shapes (no computer) This is the most important exercise of the year, and it needs neither software nor electricity. Its point is to train the eye. Look around the room, or take a few photos: a human face, a game character, a car, a building, a cup. For each object, say out loud which primitives it is made of : box, sphere, cylinder, cone, torus, plane. Next to the original, draw a simplified “skeleton” shape. Start simple: a cup is a cylinder plus a torus (the handle). Finish with something harder: a character is a cylinder or box torso, cylinder limbs, a sphere head. // who we are About the club “3D Workshop” is a modeling and 3D-printing club: from sketch to finished object, with the emphasis on everyone’s own idea. # What the club is “3D Workshop” is a modeling and 3D-printing club. We follow the whole path from sketch to finished object: creating our own 3D models, preparing them for display or printing and making the objects. The format is theory and practice, individual and team work; at the end of the year there is an exhibition and demo day of the finished projects. The club is open to college students and to anyone who wants to learn: no experience is needed, and the age range in the project plan is 15 to 35. # The new direction for 2026–2027 This year the club deliberately changes course: Less CAD and printing for the sake of souvenirs. Students already study CAD in other subjects, and printing stays as the final realization of the best projects. More polygonal modeling — this is what participants actually ask for: game characters and assets. Next in the program: topology, preparing models for game engines (Unreal Engine, Unity) and your own AR showcase. The main goal is not the software but the skill: seeing simple shapes in any object, breaking the complex into simple parts and sharpening the basics so much that moving to another editor is no problem. Self-expression comes first. Everyone works on their own idea; the leader adapts the difficulty. The full year map is on the The year’s program page. # The leader Oleksii Boichenko, leader of the “3D Workshop” club, Classical Professional College of SumDU. The schedule, announcements and contact with the leader are in the club’s Telegram group (the leader provides the invitation; the schedule for the new year is posted in the group rather than on this site, because it can change). # Organizers The club runs as part of the “Circle of Friends” project of the “Vienna” Charitable Foundation and the Classical Professional College of SumDU, supported by Welthause Graz. # About this site Bilingual. h: Session 1 — the viewport, selection, hierarchy and panels
x: 00 // Block 0 of 10 · sessions 1 The Blender interface The viewport, axis navigation, selection, the object hierarchy and property panels — before your first blockout. Duration 1 session · ~2 h each Checkpoint You confidently orbit the view, select objects and mesh elements, and find the right properties panel without being told. Challenge Find all six orthographic views on your own keyboard (with or without a numpad) and teach the trick to the person next to you. # The idea of the block Before building anything of your own, it helps to answer a boring but important question: where even am I on this screen? Blender opens with a huge number of buttons, panels and tiny icons, and trying to memorize all of them upfront is a guaranteed way to get discouraged before your first cube. The good news: you really only need four screen zones and a handful of habits , and the rest sticks as it comes up naturally. This block isn't about "what every button does." It's about not getting lost: how to spin the model around to see it from the side you need; how to select exactly the right face instead of the wrong one; where to look for an object's name once there are ten of them on the scene; where to check or change exact numbers instead of dragging the mouse and guessing. None of this belongs to any one tool from the blocks ahead — it works underneath all of them at once. Four zones worth recognizing at a glance The viewport (the big central area) — the 3D scene itself. The object hierarchy (the Outliner, top-right corner) — a list of everything on the scene. Properties (bottom-right corner) — a set of tabs with details about the selected object. The mode header (above the viewport) — the switch between Object Mode and Edit Mode, and what exactly gets selected. Blender's default window — the same four zones, live # Session 1 — the viewport, selection, hierarchy and panels Open Blender. By default the scene already has a cube, a camera and a light — don't delete them yet, they're useful landmarks for your first mouse movements. # Navigating the viewport The viewport isn't a "photo" of the scene from one fixed side — it's a window into 3D space that you can rotate, slide and zoom however you like. t: Block 1. Your first object in one session
x: 01 // Block 1 of 10 · sessions 2–3 Your first object in one session Five tools, mirror symmetry and face colors — no UV unwrapping. Duration 2 sessions · ~2 h each Checkpoint A finished, colored, symmetrical object — your first showpiece of the year. Challenge A second object with more complex symmetry, or a palette for a mood (“rusty metal” vs “neon toy”). # The idea of the block At the introductory session you already did two things: you said what you want to learn to make and you put together a rough silhouette of that idea from primitives . Block 1 is the bridge from “a pile of cubes and balls” to a first object you actually want to show: colored, detailed, made in a single evening . The technique is borrowed from game-asset blockout practice (the Imphenzia channel): five tools + the Mirror modifier + face colors without UV unwrapping . This minimal set is no accident: these five actions cover almost everything a beginner needs for a blockout, and skipping UV unwrapping removes the step where everybody usually gets stuck. You see a colored result right away, not a grey blank. The object should be symmetrical A vehicle, a weapon, a ship, a building, a creature in a calm pose — anything with a common axis. Symmetry doesn’t narrow your choice: it gives you Mirror — instantly doubled detail for half the work. This is exactly what lets you finish in a single session. The key skill of the block is recognizing the right tool from the shape of the task instead of hunting through menus at random. Before — the blockout after session 2 After — the palette from session 3 # Session 2 — the five tools Take your silhouette from the introductory session (or, if your idea has changed, start a new blockout — it takes a few minutes). Tool What it does Example Extrude E pulls a face or an edge out into new geometry pull a ship’s nose out of a starting cube Inset I creates a smaller face inside the selected one an inset for a porthole before pushing it in Bevel Ctrl + B chamfers a sharp edge, removes the “plastic” look round the corners of a hull Loop Cut Ctrl + R adds a loop of edges across a form cut a wing so you can pull out an aileron later Mirror (modifier) mirrors one half across an axis turn it on first — and forget about it Extrude E Inset I Bevel Ctrl B Loop Cut Ctrl R Mirror modifier # Each tool a bit closer up Extrude ( E ). h: Session 5 — Boolean, Merge and assembling from parts
x: 02 // Block 2 of 10 · sessions 4–5 Extended toolkit and detailing Knife, Subdivision Surface, Boolean and Merge: asymmetric forms and assembly from parts. Duration 2–3 sessions · ~2 h each Checkpoint Your object from block 1, refined and assembled from several parts. Challenge The same model with a moving part (lid, door, turret) — a separate object with its own origin. # The idea of the block The five tools of block 1 are deliberately limited — so the first session is guaranteed to give a result. But they have a limit: all they can make are forms symmetrical about one axis, with details that “stick out”. Block 2 lifts that limit with three new tools: Knife — cut the mesh freely, not only with loops across the form; Subdivision Surface — smooth an angular form into an organic one in a controlled way; Boolean and Merge — join separate parts into one model instead of only building on from one piece. Subdivision Surface is not a “beauty button” It is a tool that amplifies what is already built into the topology (the number and placement of loops). On an angular, uneven mesh it gives an angular, uneven “smooth” form. We come back to this in Block 4 . A guiding principle: break the complex into parts Behind Merge and Boolean is a strategy that becomes critical in Block 5 : a complex idea is not built as one solid piece . You split it into logical parts (for a character — head, torso, limbs, weapon; for a car — body, wheels, interior details), work on each as its own object and assemble them only at the end. That makes it easier to keep everything in your head and to fix one part without risking the whole model. # Session 4 — Knife and Subdivision Surface Knife ( K ) cuts the mesh along any line you draw with the mouse right across the model’s surface. Unlike Loop Cut, the line doesn’t have to be a straight loop around the whole form. With it you can cut an uneven seam, a hull panel, a scar, a triangular dent. Subdivision Surface adds smoothness. Look at two contrasting examples: an organic creature or a character’s head: an angular blockout → a smooth form with one modifier; a spaceship hull with crisp engineered edges: here smoothness “eats” the design, so Subdivision isn’t needed. Control the smoothing level (Levels Viewport / Render) and keep the effect as a modifier — then you can keep editing the rough “cage” instead of “baking” the result into the geometry

h: Session 6 — the reference and a blockout along the outline
x: 03 // Block 3 of 10 · sessions 6–7 Modeling from references Don’t invent proportions — check them against an image right in the viewport. Duration 3–4 sessions · ~2 h each Checkpoint Your own object (car, weapon, character, building) modeled from a reference: blockout and detailing. Challenge An object with complex symmetry or a mechanism, or your own drawn reference instead of a found photo. # The idea of the block Until now you built forms “from your head” — from imagination and memory of your own idea. That works well for simple, familiar things, but has a limit: as soon as the idea gets harder (a specific car model, a character with clear proportions, a building of a certain style), memory and your eye let you down — proportions “drift”, symmetry “by eye” turns out not to be so symmetrical. The answer is not “more talent” but a concrete technique: a reference image right in the viewport . This is what professional modelers do: they don’t invent proportions but check them against a real image, like an artist checks against a live model. You choose the object A car, a weapon, a character, a building, a creature — anything with a clear front and side view. You find or prepare the image yourself. It continues the principle of self-expression, now tied to real proportions. # Session 6 — the reference and a blockout along the outline What makes a good reference? We discuss it in pairs, and the summary is: a view strictly from the side and strictly from the front (not in perspective and not at an angle), otherwise proportions get distorted when laid over an orthographic view ; the same relative width and height of the object in both images, so you don’t fit the scale “by eye”; enough resolution to see the details you plan to model. Look for technical drawings and blueprint images for machines and reference sites for characters. No perfect “front + side” pair? Even a single view will do if the object is fairly symmetrical. Importing into the viewport . Reference/Background Images puts the image on a separate orthographic plane tied to a specific view (Front/Side). Adjust the transparency (Opacity) so you can see through it to the mesh you’re building. A typical mistake is a forgotten scale: the reference and the future model must be of comparable size from the very start. Practice: a blockout along the outline. h: Session 9 — retopology and the polygon budget
x: 04 // Block 4 of 10 · sessions 8–9 Topology and retopology Why “just making the shape” is not enough: will this mesh survive movement? Duration 2–3 sessions · ~2 h each Checkpoint Your object from block 3, checked and retopologized: clean mesh exactly where the movement will be. Challenge The same model with a deliberately reduced polygon budget (LOD thinking). # The idea of the block The “done or not” judgment was purely visual so far: it looks as intended — so it’s done. Block 4 introduces a second criterion, invisible in a screenshot: will this mesh survive movement? A model can look perfect and yet break as soon as someone tries to bend it in a game or an animation, because inside the form there is a topology with a random number of corners and triangular “fans” where a smooth bend should be. The “Clean Mesh” trainer is exactly about this: three meshes that look the same, one bend, and only one deforms predictably. Start with it: open the trainer . Through simple shapes, not abstract theory Everything is explained on circles and rectangles → loops. Every concept is immediately checked on a real bend or joint. # Session 8 — why quads matter Imagine your character has to raise an arm, or your car has to open a door. Are you sure the mesh at the bend will cope? Most people haven’t thought about it, and that’s fine: today is exactly about this. Quad, triangle or n-gon. The same form can be made of different faces: Face type What it gives The problem if it’s not where it should be Quad (4 corners) supports Loop Cut, easier UVs, predictable deformation — (this is the goal) Triangle sometimes unavoidable (a cone’s tip, an edge) a pile of triangles in a row = a pole : a point where too many edges meet; deforms badly N-gon (5+ corners) quickly closes a big flat area doesn’t support Subdivision and Loop Cut predictably, especially in a bend zone Edge flow . Edge loops should run around a joint, like rings around a finger, not through it. The MatCap check. In Viewport Shading → Solid pick a reflective MatCap instead of the flat material. On a bad, uneven mesh reflections “swim” and distort unevenly, on a clean one they lie smoothly. It’s a quick visual test you can do at any stage of the work. Practice: diagnose your own object. h: Session 13 — a hierarchy for the pose
x: 05 // Block 5 of 10 · sessions 10–14 Your own game object — the flagship project The biggest project of the half-year, from your own idea: silhouette, details, palette, pose. Duration 4–5 sessions · ~2 h each Checkpoint A finished, presentable object — the portfolio piece of the first half of the year. Challenge A simple pose or expression (characters) or a functional moving part (props, weapons). # The idea of the block This is the biggest project of the half-year. Unlike the previous blocks, there is no new toolset here : everything you need (five tools, detailing, references, topology) you already have from blocks 1–4. The leader’s role shifts from “show a new technique” to coaching and pacing. You choose your own idea from day one — a character, a weapon or a prop: what you named at the introductory session, or changed since — and bring it to a presentable state. The path follows Grant Abbitt’s structure: silhouette from simple shapes → detailing → texture palette → a basic hierarchy for a pose . The same path smaller objects already took in blocks 1–3, only now on the most ambitious idea of the year. Everyone’s pace is their own The question you’ll be asked in every session is always the same: “What shapes is this made of, and what is still missing?” If needed, you’ll be reminded of a specific tool from earlier blocks rather than shown a new one. Break down → work on the parts → assemble at the end The flagship project is the first truly complex model of the year, and the principle from Block 2 becomes here a survival strategy for the project. Before you build the silhouette as one object, split your idea into 3–5 logical parts (preferably on paper). Each part is a separate object: you can detail it, fix it or even redo it from scratch without risking the rest. Assembly through Merge , Boolean or Parent is the last step, not the first. # Session 10 — the silhouette First everyone names their idea or confirms the one they had. If the idea has grown into something too big for five sessions, narrow the scope, not the topic: not “less of a character” but “today this detail, not the whole set of armor”. Split the idea into parts right away: name on paper or out loud 3–5 parts (a character: head, torso, arms, legs, a weapon or accessory; a car: body, wheels, cabin). This is the plan you’ll build by. Session 16 — the motion loop and cleaning the weights
x: 06 // Block 6 of 10 · sessions 15–16 Rigging in 15 minutes (and a bit more) One repeatable Rigify sequence to bring your own object to life with a simple loop. Duration 2–3 sessions · ~2 h each Checkpoint Your block 5 object, animated with a simple loop (walk, spin, open) through a rig you built yourself. Challenge Understand bone layers and tidy them up on your own. # The idea of the block “Rigging” sounds like a separate profession that takes years to study — and at depth, it is. But to bring one specific object to life with a simple motion loop you don’t need animation theory; you need one repeatable sequence of actions that you can go through for the first time in 15 minutes and repeat on your own object a second time, already deliberately. This is Grant Abbitt’s technique: a Rigify meta-rig → fitting the bones → generating the final rig → Automatic Weights → cleaning up the bone layers. Rig for a specific movement Rigging is preparation for a movement you already imagine (session 13 of block 5 asked about it). Don’t rig “just in case”: rig for a specific pose or loop. # Session 15 — Rigify: the meta-rig and generation First remind yourself of the planned movement from block 5 . Then six steps you go through on your own object: Step Action Why 1 Enable the Rigify add-on (Edit → Preferences → Add-ons) gives ready-made “meta-rig” templates: you don’t build every bone by hand 2 Add a meta-rig that matches the object’s form (human, a simple biped or your own simple armature of a few bones) a starting frame that you then fit to the model 3 Move the meta-rig’s bones so they line up with the model’s joints (elbows, knees, hinges) bones must lie inside the mesh exactly where bending happens 4 Generate the final rig (the Generate Rig button) Rigify turns the meta-rig into a full control system with controllers 5 Bind the model to the rig via Parent with Automatic Weights ( Ctrl + P ) Blender itself works out which part of the mesh moves with which bone 6 Hide the extra bone layers (Bone Layers) leave visible only the controllers you’ll really use Practice. Add the simplest meta-rig that matches the intended movement (not necessarily a full human skeleton: a few bones are often enough) and go through steps 3–5 on your object from block 5. Challenge Understand the bone-layer structure and tidy up on your own (step 6), without waiting for help. # Session 16 — the mo

x: 07 // Block 7 of 10 · sessions 17–18 Preparing a model for a game engine Three things that break an export: transforms, scale and normals. Duration 2–3 sessions · ~2 h each Checkpoint The model is exported in a format for your target (engine or web) and verified: scale and normals are intact. Challenge Compare the model’s Dimensions with the real-world size of the thing you imagined. # The idea of the block The model has lived entirely inside Blender so far. Block 7 is about the last step, which often fails precisely because it seems a formality: a correct export . A model that looks perfect in Blender can arrive in another application a hundred times smaller, turned on its side or with black faces instead of color. The cause is always one of three: transforms, scale, normals . The checklist is shared, the format isn’t Some prepare a model for Unity or Unreal (a future game portfolio), others for their own AR showcase in block 8 (web, GLB). The checklist is the same, the file format differs by target. # Session 17 — three things that break an export A live illustration: a model deliberately left unprepared (transforms not applied), right after being imported into a test environment, looks deformed or the wrong size. This is what will happen to your model if you skip the checklist. 1. Apply Transform . Object → Apply → All Transforms. There is the “visible” size and rotation of an object and its real internal data (Scale, Rotation) shown in the N-panel. If you don’t apply them, the receiving engine can interpret these numbers its own way, and the object will “drift”. 2. Units and scale. The key fact of 2026: Blender 5.x is metric by default ( 1 unit = 1 meter ), while Unreal Engine counts in centimeters. A cube with a side of “1” in Blender is a meter: roughly a person’s height, not a house and not a button. If it looks wrong by eye, that’s the signal to check the scale before exporting. 3. Names. Meaningful names for objects and materials instead of Cube.004 . Practice: the checklist on your own object. Go through your model: Apply Transform; check the scale (does the object look a reasonable size next to a standard 1-meter cube); check the names. Challenge Work out how the N-panel shows Dimensions in real units (meters/centimeters) and compare your object with the real size of the thing you imagined: a sword shouldn’t be as tall as a house. # Session 18 — n

x: 08 // Block 8 of 10 · sessions 19–20 An AR showcase without special hardware Your own model in augmented reality on your own phone — via a link or a QR code. Duration 2 sessions · ~2 h each Checkpoint The model opens in AR via a link or QR code; shown live “on the table” through the camera. Challenge Tune the angle and lighting (auto-rotate, camera-orbit) so the model shows its best side right away. # The idea of the block Last year “VR” in the club’s program meant a conditional item “if the equipment is available”, dependent on whether there was a headset in the room. This year it is replaced by a concrete, always-available result: augmented reality straight from your phone , no app and no special hardware — just a link or a QR code. The technical basis is the model-viewer web component (developed by Google): you put a GLB model into an ordinary web page, and on a phone AR mode opens with one tap: Quick Look on iOS, Scene Viewer on Android. That’s how furniture stores offer to “see how this chair will look in your room”. This is a personal thing The result of the block is not an abstract demonstration of a technology but your own model, made with your own hands, in augmented reality on your own phone. # Session 19 — model-viewer and the first launch A page with <model-viewer> is a few lines of HTML, not a program: a web page with a GLB file and a “View in AR” button. The component detects the visitor’s device and picks the right way to show it: Quick Look for iPhone, Scene Viewer for Android, an ordinary rotating view for a computer. Practice: your own page with a model. Take the .glb file from block 7 and drop it into the ready-made template: the AR showcase template . In pairs if there aren’t enough laptops. The goal of the session is to see your model in the browser and rotate it with the mouse. AR mode on the phone comes next time, once the page is published and available by link: AR needs a real internet address , not just a file on your computer. Challenge Choose the angle and lighting ( auto-rotate , camera-orbit ) so the model “shows itself” from its best side as soon as the page opens. # Session 20 — AR on the phone Warm-up. Make sure the page from last time is published ( GitHub Pages ) and reachable by link, not just a local file: this is a necessary condition for AR. The QR code. x: 09 // Block 9 of 10 · sessions 21–23 The final project and your portfolio page One finished, well-documented project — and a page you can proudly show outside the club. Duration 2–3 sessions · ~2 h each Checkpoint A published portfolio page: a GLB model, screenshots of the journey and a short description. Challenge Prepare and rehearse a live talk for demo day (1–2 minutes). # The idea of the block The end of the year should give you something more concrete than a “show in a session”: a portfolio page you can show outside the club — to parents, a college or university admissions committee, a future employer. One of the year’s projects (most often the flagship object from block 5 , already animated and shown in AR) is brought to a presentable state and laid out on your own page of the club’s site ( GitHub Pages ): a GLB model through model-viewer , screenshots of the intermediate checkpoints, a short description of the path from silhouette to finished result. Choose the project that represents you best It needn’t be the flagship. If you are prouder of another object, that is an acceptable choice too. What matters is one finished, well-documented project , not a cursory overview of the whole year. This block is deliberately open: the number of sessions is flexible (roughly 2–3), and the pace and content depend on where you have got to by the end of the year. There are no new tools. # Session 21 — choosing a project and final polish First say which project of the year will be the basis of the page and one thing you want to improve in it. Then an open workshop: refine the chosen project with the whole toolkit of the year (detailing, color, topology, rig). At the end, note down: do you already have a GLB export ( block 7 ) and an AR page ( block 8 )? If so, it’s a ready foundation and only the layout remains; if not, that is the priority for the next session. # Session 22 — the portfolio page The structure of a good page: the project’s title ; a GLB model through <model-viewer> (the same as in block 8); 3–4 screenshots of the journey : silhouette → details → color → final (this is where _step1.blend , _step2.blend … come in handy); a short description : what the project is, the hardest part, what you learned. Take the AR showcase template as your base: drop in the model, add screenshots and text. Checkpoint A published portfolio page with a GLB model, screenshots

// practice between sessions Exercises Short interactive exercises run right in the browser: nothing to install, no sign-up, no tracking. The exercises are designed for 5–15 minutes and complement the sessions. Each one is tied to a block of the program: the exercise page shows exactly where it helps and which terms are worth knowing. Trainers (See the Shape, Clean Mesh) open full-screen and work on a computer and on a phone. Your score and streak are stored only in your browser. Templates (the AR showcase) are ready-made pages that you copy and fill with your own model. You can change an exercise’s language in its top corner; by default it matches the site’s language. Idea The list will grow during the year: the next exercises are about color and palette (block 1) and checking proportions against a reference (block 3). trainer See the Shape Break an object into simple shapes and find the true rotation of a figure, not its mirror image. Spatial thinking · Block 1 trainer Clean Mesh Three meshes, one bend: pick the one that deforms predictably instead of breaking or forming a pole. // trainer · Spatial thinking See the Shape Break an object into simple shapes and find the true rotation of a figure, not its mirror image. Open the exercise # What it trains The skill the club works on all year: seeing simple shapes inside a complex object and telling a true rotation of a figure from its mirror image. The first is the basis of a blockout ( Block 1 ); the second is understanding how Mirror works. # Two modes “Break it into shapes.” In front of you is a three-dimensional object (a mug, a lamp, a rocket, a robot, a mushroom, a chess pawn…). Rotate it with the mouse or your finger and mark every type of primitive you see: box, sphere, cylinder, cone, torus, plane. The number of repeats doesn’t matter — only the types. “Update the rotation.” On the left is the target, on the right three candidates. One is the same figure, just rotated; another is its mirror image ; the third is a completely different figure. Rotate both the target and the candidates: a true rotation matches the target cube for cube, while in a mirror image the colored cubes land in the opposite order however you turn it. # Tips In mode 1, find the biggest shape first, then whatever is “attached” to it. That is exactly what you do in a blockout. In mode 2, don’t compare figures “by eye” in one position: rotate them until one cube matches the target, then check the rest. A mirror image can’t be obtained by rotation — which is why Mirror in Blender gives you a new half, not a “rotated” old one. Note Your score and streak are stored only in your browser. The exercise language matches the site’s language; you can change it with the UA/EN buttons in the exercise’s top corner. Supports blocks Block 1 — Your first object in one session All exercises

// trainer · Topology Clean Mesh Three meshes, one bend: pick the one that deforms predictably instead of breaking or forming a pole. Open the exercise # What it trains The ability to see, before any animation, whether a mesh will survive movement . A model can look perfect and still break the moment you bend it. The exercise illustrates the topic of Block 4 with a moving picture instead of a static slide. # How it works You see three panels that bend by the same angle at the same moment . The form is the same everywhere; only the rows of loops on it differ. Pick the one whose mesh deforms predictably. What you’ll see Why Even loops exactly in the bend zone — clean quads this is the right answer: a quad mesh and edge flow around the bend Just as many loops as the correct mesh — only in the wrong place dense on the flat stretches, only three right in the bend: the count isn’t the problem, the placement is A triangular fan pole exactly in the bend zone the worst possible place for a pole: the mesh “twists” unpredictably # What we take from it A beautiful shape is no guarantee: check the mesh on a real bend. What matters here is not how many loops you have, but where they are. The second option has exactly as many loops as the correct one — they just sit where the surface is already flat, not where it bends. Edge loops should run around a joint, like rings around a finger, not through it. A quick by-eye test in Blender is MatCap : on a bad mesh the reflections “swim”. In the session we go through 2–3 rounds together out loud, and then everyone diagnoses their own object from block 3 . Note Your score and streak are stored only in your browser. You can change the language with the UA/EN buttons in the exercise’s top corner. Supports blocks Block 4 — Topology and retopology All exercises

// template · Publishing and AR AR showcase template A ready-made <model-viewer> page: drop in your own .glb model, publish it and open it in AR on your phone. Open the template Download the template # What it is A ready-made page with the model-viewer web component. You drop in your own GLB model and publish the page — it rotates in the browser and, on a phone, opens in augmented reality with one tap. We’ll use the same starting point for the portfolio page in block 9 . # How to use it Download the template and put your file next to it named model.glb (or change src="…" in the code to your own filename). Replace the text in alt="…" : briefly describe the model for people who can’t see the image. Replace the “Project name” and description placeholders under the viewport with yours: what the project is, the hardest part, what you learned. Publish the page (for example on GitHub Pages ). On a local file the AR button won’t work: you need a real https://… link. Make a QR code for the published address and scan it with your phone. # The minimal code Everything needed for viewing and AR is a few lines of HTML: Copy <script type="module" src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@google/model-viewer/dist/model-viewer.min.js"></script> <model-viewer src="model.glb" alt="A short description of the model" camera-controls auto-rotate ar ar-modes="webxr scene-viewer quick-look" shadow-intensity="1"> </model-viewer> The template already contains this code, the styling and a demo model, so the page works right away — before you swap in your own. # Before you publish Checklist Scale and Apply Transform are checked ( Block 7 ): the model doesn’t look too big or too small in AR. Normals are recalculated: no black or missing faces. The page is published (not a local file) — otherwise the AR button won’t appear on the phone. Watch out Generate the QR code only after publishing , for the final https://… address. A code pointing to localhost or a local file leads nowhere. Supports blocks Block 8 — An AR showcase without special hardware Block 9 — The final project and your portfolio page All exercises

Bakes an object’s scale, rotation and location into its geometry (Object → Apply → All Transforms). Without it Boolean, Merge and exports can go wrong.
Showing a 3D model “in real space” through a phone camera. On iOS it is Quick Look, on Android Scene Viewer; no separate app is needed.
A skeleton of bones that moves a model’s mesh. You build it for a specific movement you already imagine.
Chamfers a sharp edge ( Ctrl + B ) and removes the “plastic” look of a low-poly form.
A rough build of a form from simple blocks with no detailing. The goal is the proportions of the whole, not beauty.
A modifier that cuts or adds volume using the shape of another object. Fast but fragile: it often leaves a messy mesh.
A harder version of the same task for those who finish sooner or already have experience. Not a separate track — an add-on.
The real artifact a block ends with. Keep intermediate versions as separate files ( _step1.blend , _step2.blend ) so you can catch up on anything you missed.
A modifier that quickly simplifies a mesh that is too heavy. A rough option, not a substitute for manual retopology.
The direction of edge loops. They should run around a joint, like rings around a finger, not through it.
Pulls a face or an edge out into new geometry ( E ). This is how a nose, a bump or a barrel “grows” from a cube.
The most proven format for the Unity and Unreal Engine game engines.
Free hosting for static pages. The club’s site lives there — and so will your portfolio pages and AR showcases.
A compact 3D file format that opens reliably right in the browser. Good for the web, Godot and your own AR showcase.
Creates a smaller face inside the selected one ( I ) — it prepares an area for the next Extrude.
A saved position of an object at a given moment in time. A few keyframes make a simple motion loop.
Cuts the mesh along any line you draw across the surface ( K ). Unlike Loop Cut, the line doesn’t have to be a straight loop.
Different levels of detail for different parts or distances: a face seen up close deserves more polygons than a shoe sole.
Adds a loop of edges across a form ( Ctrl + R ) — an area for local detailing.
A shading mode with a reflective material and no textures. On a bad mesh the reflections “swim” — a quick visual test of topology.
A description of a surface’s color and look. Assigning materials to faces colors the model without UV unwrapping. Export needs a real material with a Base Color.
Joins vertices or separate objects into one mesh ( M → At Center / By Distance). A simple, reliable way to assemble a model from parts.
A modifier that mirrors half of an object across an axis: edit one half and both are done. Turn it on first.
A Google web component: it puts a GLB model into an ordinary page and opens AR on a phone with one tap.
A non-destructive operation on a mesh (Mirror, Subdivision Surface, Boolean, Shrinkwrap, Decimate). You can change or disable it until it is applied.
A face with five or more corners. It quickly fills a flat area but deforms poorly, especially in a bend zone.
The directions faces “look” in. A face with a wrong normal turns black or disappears after export. The quick fix is Recalculate ( Shift + N ).
The object’s pivot point for rotation and scaling. Mirror, moving parts and rigs all depend on it.
A view without perspective (Front, Side, Top). These are the images you need as references, because perspective distorts proportions.
A “parent — child” link between objects ( Ctrl + P ). A moving part then rotates about the right point, not an arbitrary one.
A vertex where too many edges meet (typically a triangle “fan”). Bad in a bend zone because the mesh deforms unpredictably there.
The simplest ready-made 3D shape: box, sphere, cylinder, cone, torus, plane. Every blockout starts with primitives.
An image a phone scans to open a link. Generate it only for a published https:// address, never for a local file.
A four-sided face. The basis of a clean mesh: it supports Loop Cut, Subdivision and predictable deformation.
An image you check your model against: front view, side view, blueprint. Real proportions instead of “by eye”.
Building a new clean mesh over an old form — by hand or with help from Shrinkwrap and Decimate.
A Blender add-on with ready-made rig templates (meta-rig → Generate Rig). It gets you a result in one session without building every bone by hand.
A modifier that pulls a new clean mesh onto the surface of an old form. Place it above Mirror and Subdivision in the stack.
The outline of an object that reads at a single glance. If the silhouette isn’t recognizable, details won’t save it.
A modifier that smooths an angular form into an organic one. It is not a “beauty button”: it amplifies the topology you already have — messy or clean.
How the mesh is built inside a form: how many and what kind of faces, where the loops run. It decides whether a model survives bending.
Flattening a 3D model onto a plane, like an apple’s peel, so you can paint a texture on it. The club deliberately skips it at the start.
Painting directly on vertices or faces — another way to get color without UV unwrapping.
The Blender window where you see and edit the 3D scene.
Painting by hand which part of the mesh belongs to which bone. A quick patch for places where Automatic Weights got it wrong.
